title: TCS unit HyperVault plans $7.4 billion, 1 GW AI campus in Hyderabad
subtitle: Tata's AI infrastructure subsidiary secured 264 acres in Telangana for what would be one of India's largest single AI investments.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: HyperVault, a subsidiary of Tata Consultancy Services, announced on September 5 that it will invest up to ₹700 billion — about $7.41 billion — to build a 1 GW AI data center campus in Hyderabad, in the state of Telangana. The company has secured 264 acres and will develop the site in phases tied to customer demand rather than delivering the full gigawatt from day one. The campus is designed to serve hyperscalers and AI companies running high-density GPU workloads for training and inference.

The scale of the commitment is the point. India has attracted large data center pledges before, but the vast majority have been sub-500 MW and split across multiple sites. A single 1 GW campus lets a hyperscaler place a foundation-model training run in India for the first time, without slicing the workload across geographies. It also puts Telangana ahead of Maharashtra and Tamil Nadu in the state-level competition for AI infrastructure that has intensified since Maharashtra's ₹10,000 crore AI policy in August.

Power, not real estate, is the harder problem — and the reason the buildout is phased. Telangana's grid is already among the most stressed in India during summer peaks, and 1 GW of AI load is roughly the demand of a mid-sized Indian city running flat out. Tata will have to negotiate captive generation, long-term PPAs, or both, before the site can absorb its full nameplate. That negotiation is where the deal will actually be won or lost, and it is where every gigawatt-class AI campus globally now spends most of its time.

For learners: when you see a headline gigawatt data center announcement, look past the dollar figure to the power question. How is the site interconnected? What is the source? What is the customer's cost per kilowatt-hour committed for how many years? The compute economics of AI at this scale are 60–70% electricity, and the deal terms on power are what determine whether the campus is competitive or a stranded asset.
